story.title: Apple Launches M6 iMac, Entry MacBook Pro Ahead of Touch Laptop - Bloomberg.com

facts.text: Apple is targeting the MacBook Pro at everyone from college students to business users and creators, while the iMac is meant for families and small-business users.
Apple ( AAPL ) debuted two new Macs on Tuesday as it continues to refresh its lineup of devices amid a flurry of announcements this fall.
The company showed off a new 14-inch MacBook Pro and an iMac , both with its M6 chips, which it launched in August.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Apple's Mac line of devices accounted for $33.7 billion of the company's $416.1 billion in 2025, making it the tech giant's fourth-largest segment by sales.
The Macs come a day after Apple debuted its newest iPad mini, which received a larger, improved display and new processor.
The company is expected to cap off its announcements on Wednesday with the launch of its first-ever touchscreen-equipped MacBook.
Apple has stepped up the cadence of product launches in the second half of the year, bringing out everything from new processors and desktops to AirPods, watches, and more.
On Monday, Apple responded to early reports of some Duo displays breaking along the hinge, saying that it is aware of the matter and urging users to contact Apple support for replacement devices.
Apple has rolled out a new 24-inch iMac and an entry-level MacBook Pro with a 14-inch screen, marking key updates in an end-to-end overhaul of the company’s computer line.
Apple said the M6 chip makes the iMac five times faster than the prior model from 2024 for artificial intelligence, while the new MacBook Pro is 30% speedier than its predecessor for graphics.
Beyond the push into touchscreen displays, Apple is preparing a refreshed MacBook Neo and MacBook Air for the first half of 2027 .
It is planning an M7 Ultra and a new Mac Studio in 2028.
The company continues to sell higher-end M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros, which have more advanced main processing and graphics cores compared with the entry M6 machines.
This week, Apple released a series of new products in rapid succession, launching the 24-inch iMac and 14-inch entry-level MacBook Pro with the M6 chip ahead of the touchscreen MacBook Pro's debut.
This round of intensive updates is part of Apple’s broader product roadmap.
On Monday, the company updated the iPad mini with an upgraded display and water-resistant features.
Two new models will be available for pre-order at 1:10 AM on October 29, with official shipping beginning on November 6.
The new iMac starts at RMB 12,499, and the MacBook Pro starts at RMB 15,999.

Apple is continuing its comprehensive overhaul of its computer lineup to meet growing demands for artificial intelligence applications; the two new products released today are milestones in this journey, not the final destination.
Apple has scheduled a product showcase in Los Angeles for October 28, where it is expected to unveil its first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen.
The redesigned laptop is reportedly getting an OLED display, a slimmer and lighter body, and a Dynamic Island-style cutout.
Apple is also preparing an updated iMac with a new M6 chip and additional color options, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.
They will remain available alongside the new touchscreen versions for a time, giving customers a less expensive alternative.
The new OLED models are expected to use Apple's existing M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, which debuted in March.
Their main upgrades will therefore be the display, design and input options rather than a new generation of chips.

The more expensive OLED panels could also push starting prices up by as much as $500 compared with current models, which start at $2,499 for the 14-inch version and $2,999 for the 16-inch model in the US.
The switch to OLED should bring deeper blacks and higher contrast than the mini-LED panels used in current MacBook Pro models.
Apple is reportedly working on changes to macOS to make touch input feel more natural without turning the Mac into an oversized iPad.
For example, touching a button could bring up a menu with larger controls positioned around the user's finger.
